subject: Architecture
title: Passive Solar Design: Free Heating and Cooling
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Passive Solar Design: Free Heating and Cooling.

hook.text: Ancient Romans oriented their bathhouses to catch afternoon sun. We forgot that trick for centuries.

buildup.text: Passive solar design positions windows, walls, and floors to collect, store, and distribute sun warmth.

discovery.text: South-facing windows in the Northern Hemisphere capture winter sun while roof overhangs block summer heat.

twist.text: Thermal mass — concrete or stone floors — absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night for free.

climax.text: Well-designed passive solar homes can reduce heating bills by 50-70% with zero mechanical systems.

punchline.text: The best heating system is a window pointed in the right direction.

quiz.question: How much can passive solar design reduce heating costs?

details.summary: Passive solar design uses building orientation, window placement, thermal mass, and shading to capture winter sun for heating and block summer sun for cooling — all without mechanical systems.
details.whyItMatters: Passive solar design costs almost nothing extra at the design stage but delivers free heating and cooling for the building's entire lifespan. It proves that the cheapest energy is energy you never need to generate.
takeaways: Orientation and window placement capture winter sun, block summer sun
Thermal mass stores heat during the day and releases it at night
Roof overhangs shade high summer sun while admitting low winter sun

faq.question: How does passive solar heating work in winter?
faq.answer: Large south-facing windows admit low-angle winter sunlight that strikes thermal mass floors and walls. These dense materials absorb heat during sunny hours and radiate it back at night. Properly designed passive solar homes can provide 50-70% of their heating from sunlight alone.

faq.question: Does passive solar work in cloudy climates?
faq.answer: It works less dramatically but still helps. Even overcast skies provide diffuse light and some warmth. In cloudy climates, passive solar design focuses more on daylighting to reduce electric lighting needs and on heavy insulation to retain whatever solar gain occurs.
